headline_marked: Intel's [[18A-P process]] enters risk production, promising 9% performance boost
headline: Intel's 18A-P process enters risk production, promising 9% performance boost
summary: Intel's enhanced 18A-P node offers a 9% performance increase at iso-power or an 18% power reduction at iso-performance, with improved thermal resistance.
details: Intel has revealed more details about its performance-optimized 18A-P process, an enhancement of the 18A node. This new process promises a 9% improvement in performance at the same power consumption, or an 18% reduction in power at the same performance level. It has now entered risk production, a crucial stage before mass manufacturing.

Risk production involves low-volume manufacturing on a standard production line to gather data on defect rates, performance, and variability. While typically preceding mass production by 12-24 months, the timeline for 18A-P may be tighter as it's an enhancement rather than a completely new node.

The 18A-P process is backward compatible with existing 18A designs, allowing for easy porting. It introduces new transistor designs, including W1.5 and the enhanced W3P with 'Power Boost,' which utilizes backside power delivery to reduce parasitic resistance and increase switching speed.

Intel has also added a new ULVTLL (Ultra-Low Voltage Threshold Low Leakage) VT pair to its lineup. This option offers a balance between performance and power leakage, providing chip designers with greater flexibility when creating new processors.

Beyond performance gains, the 18A-P revision boasts a 20% to 40% improvement in thermal resistance. This enhancement is critical for managing heat in high-performance computing applications, potentially leading to more efficient and powerful processors.

headline_marked: [[Nearly a fifth]] of Steam Next Fest demos disclose generative AI use
headline: Nearly a fifth of Steam Next Fest demos disclose generative AI use
summary: A significant portion of game demos at Steam Next Fest are now tagged with generative AI disclosures, reflecting a growing trend and player scrutiny in the industry.
details: At the recent Steam Next Fest, a notable 19.5% of the showcased game demos, totaling 1,704 out of 8,700 titles, have disclosed the use of generative AI. This high prevalence highlights the increasing integration of AI in game development.

The disclosure rate is significant given the mixed reception AI-generated content has received from players and indie developers. Valve updated its Steam guidelines in 2024 to require developers to inform players about the use of generative AI in their games.

While Valve's updated guidelines allow for "efficiency gains" to not necessarily warrant an AI label, some developers have faced backlash for using AI assets that were not replaced before launch, as seen with titles like Crimson Desert. This has led to increased transparency demands.

Even games that initially embraced AI from their inception, such as Arc Raiders, have reportedly scaled back their use of the technology in recent months, indicating a cautious approach to AI integration in the gaming community.
